label: Corning ADSS 72F aerial, G.652.D
notes: Corning 072ELE-T3322A20 product spec sheet (Corning Optical Communications ecatalog, product specification 072ELE-T3322A20_EMEA_AEN, revision date 2026-11-28): 'Aerial Dielectric Self-Supporting Cable, ADSS 72 F, Single-mode (OS2), A-D2Y(T)2Y, (6 x 12)'. Six active loose tubes of 12 fibres in twelve tube positions with six filling elements (the Cable Design block prints 12 tube positions, 6 active tubes, 6 filling elements, 12 fibres per tube), dielectric central element, DRY core held by swellable elements rather than gel, non-metallic (aramid) strength members over the core, black PE jacket, halogen-free, one ripcord; construction A-D2Y(T)2Y per EN 60794-1-1 (DIN VDE 0888-100-1); 15.1 mm nominal diameter, 161 kg/km, crush 3000 N/10 cm, max tensile 1700 N long-term / 4000 N short-term, min bend radius 265 mm installation / 225 mm operation, -5 to +50 C installation and -40 to +70 C operation and storage, Telcordia/TIA-598 tube colours (blue, orange, green, brown, slate, white, red, black, yellow, violet, rose, aqua), ITU-T G.652.D / IEC 60793-2-50 B1.3 fibre, cable cutoff 1260 nm, PMD link design value <= 0.06 ps/sqrt(km), and max cable length per reel/drum 6000 m. The 15.1 mm and 161 kg/km figures are the same numbers the 12F and 24F sheets print for this construction, because Corning builds one stranded core across the small rungs and the diameter does not grow with the count until the 96F sheet's 19.9 mm / 198 kg/km. Why the row exists: the aerial family shipped 12/24/48 and then 96/144 (g652d-adss-12, -24, -48, -96, -144), so the rungs skip 72, and cableFor's smallest-that-fits rule has no aerial answer between 48 and 96 fibres. Measured on this engine before the row: cableForSpan(60, 1200, ['g652d-adss-144', 'g652d-adss-96', 'g652d-adss-48'], registry) answers g652d-adss-96 - twenty-four to thirty-six fibres of aerial cable nobody asked for on a 1.2 km pole run - and a ladder that carries the duct rung instead (['g652d-adss-48', 'g652d-loose-72']) answers g652d-loose-72, a gel-filled duct cable named for a pole route. With this row in the ladder the same 60-fibre call answers g652d-adss-72. The size is not a corner case: a 36-house active tree (8 x 6 grid, two strands per ONT) routed on an aerial ladder measured 210,393.6 fibre-metres before this row and 169,504.8 after, because six spans move from the 96F rung to this one - the 1,334.3 m trunk carrying 72 strands and the 120.1 m span carrying 60, plus the 83.1 m spans carrying 58, 56 and 54 - which is 40,888.8 fibre-metres of cable bought for nothing (24 spare fibres x 1,703.7 m of span length across those six spans; lengths are summed raw rather than x1.03 because a fibre-metre is fibre count x measured span length). Cable metres, design metres and drum count are unchanged at 4,463.8 / 4,597.7 / 5: over-fibring is paid for in fibre-metres, the term a cable price tracks. Attenuation, and exactly what kind of figure it is: the sheet publishes MAXIMUM 0.36 dB/km at 1310 nm, 0.36 at 1383 nm and 0.22 at 1550 nm - maxima, not typicals, and no 1490 nm figure at all. This row carries 0.35 / 0.22 / 0.21, the same typical installed row every other cable here carries, deliberately: budgeting one aerial span at a factory maximum while its duct neighbours are budgeted at typicals prices the same design two different ways. 1490 nm is interpolated between the two published windows and is not a citation from Corning or from ITU-T. The published 0.36 at 1310 nm sits 0.01 dB/km above the 0.35 here, so hold the supplier to 0.36 in the acceptance test and read the as-built OTDR for a budget that gets signed. The row publishes NO drumM: Corning prints 'Max. cable length per reel/drum 6000 m' in its Dimensions block, a ceiling rather than a putup list, and carrying it would bill a 6 km reel for a short aerial span - measured on engine/length.js at 0.7 km of route that is 6,000 m of cable bought against 2,000 m at the engine default, and at 12 km 18,000 m against 14,000, the two agreeing only between 4.8 and 6 km. With no drumM the engine falls back to the engine/length.js default of 2,000 m and the BOM row carries 2,000 m with no field saying whether that is a drum or the engine default, so enter the reel actually ordered. What the engine does not model, and one trap. CABLE_USES has no 'aerial' value, so aerial-ness lives in the tags and this note and nothing in the planner reads it; no span, sag, ice or wind loading check exists, so a design will hang this cable over any span you draw and the pole-to-pole distance stays the planner's decision; nothing metallic means nothing to bond or earth at a joint, a fact rather than a field. The trap is the tie-break: cableFor answers with the SMALLEST cable that fits and breaks an equal fibre count on model id, and 'g652d-adss-72' sorts before 'g652d-loose-72' (measured: cableForSpan(72, 1200, ['g652d-loose-72', 'g652d-adss-72'], registry) answers this row), so a ladder naming both buys aerial cable for every 72-fibre span in the plant - name this row instead of its duct twin, not beside it, unless the whole plant is on poles. DEFAULT_LADDER in engine/design.js names no aerial rung, so this row reaches a design only when the caller's ladder names it: a design synthesised on the default ladder is unchanged by the part. This row deliberately does not say drop: isDropCable in engine/design.js reads the use field to REFUSE a span that ended up on drop cable beyond 300 m or bundled, and an aerial feeder is not tight-buffer G.657.A2 flat drop - use says feeder and distribution, which is what a 72F aerial span is for. One product data sheet's figures, not a measured build: replace with the cable actually purchased and its as-built attenuation before ordering.
